rationale: A wins because it turns one announcement into four usable beats and tells the founder exactly what proof would make each survive a reporter. Its "Calm's trial shows an 18% anxiety-score drop. The fine print is \"regular users\" and \"self-reported.\"" is the right skeptical posture; B's "Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" wanders into an accusation the update does not earn. B has usable material, especially the money angle, but A keeps its hands cleaner.
gaps_in_A: "pointing to a randomized trial as the reason" goes a half-step beyond the supplied facts; the update says the study is being published, not that insurers used it as their rationale.
"Meditation apps cross from wellness perk to insurer-covered benefit" risks category overreach from one Calm deal unless an insurer confirms this is a true covered benefit, not a wellness add-on.
"Your health plan may now include Calm Premium at no cost. Here is how to check." is a good service shape, but without insurer names and activation steps it is still an empty how-to.
gaps_in_B: "default benefit for 25 million Americans" invents default status and geography; the facts only say an estimated 25 million members of three national insurers get no-cost Calm Premium.
"benefits/HR trade reporter" and "employer and payer mental-health benefit design" assume employer-sponsored plan facts the update does not provide.
"instead of paying for real anxiety care" and "parity obligations" are prosecutorial premises with no supplied fact showing Calm replaces therapy, affects parity, or changes clinical coverage.
The study proof list asks for "sample size and dropout rate" but misses the killer qualifier: "regular users" needs per-protocol versus intention-to-treat scrutiny.
